The Artifact

This is an 8-page digital zine about data labeling, the hidden work of tagging and reading data so AI models can learn. It follows the suggested structure. The cover asks "Who taught the machine?" Page 2 explains what labeling is. Page 3 shows who does the work: a chain from OpenAI to Sama to about 36 workers in Kenya. Page 4 describes one nine-hour shift. Page 5 compares pay and profits, including the $12.50 hourly billing rate against the $1.32 to $2 workers took home. Page 6 uses Mar Hicks's "cis-tem" idea to show how the labor stays invisible. Page 7 gives five actions readers can take. Page 8 lists sources and credits.

Research Notes (≈300 words)

I built this zine mostly from one investigation and two academic studies. The anchor source is Billy Perrigo's 2023 TIME report on Sama and OpenAI. It gave me the wages, shift length, team size, and the disagreement between workers and Sama about counseling. For Mechanical Turk, I used Hara et al. (2018), which found a median wage of about $2 an hour, and Toxtli, Suri, and Savage (2021), which found workers spend a median 33% of their time on unpaid work. Fortune's June 2025 report gave me the Meta and Scale AI numbers. The idea of "ghost work" comes from Gray and Suri's book, and the "cis-tem" framing comes from Mar Hicks in class.

The hardest part to find was the money trail. OpenAI's side is thin. TIME says the contracts totaled about $200,000, but OpenAI later put it closer to $150,000, and the $12.50 hourly billing rate appears only in TIME. Sama also disputes some of TIME's figures, so the zine shows both sets side by side. I could not find what Scale AI pays its workers in a source I trusted, so I left that number out. Fairwork has a rating page for Scale's Remotasks, but I could not read a clear score from it, so the zine points readers to Fairwork without quoting a number.

What surprised me most was the size of the gap. Workers took home $1.32 to $2 an hour while the billing rate was $12.50, and the whole Kenya project cost about $200,000. Meta paid $14.3 billion for 49% of a data-labeling company. That ratio is what I wanted a reader to see first. The other surprise was the unpaid third of the day on Mechanical Turk. Low pay is not only a low rate. It is also time nobody counts.

Design Statement (≈250 words)

I chose a digital zine because a zine is built for this kind of topic. It is small, cheap to share, and says what big platforms would rather skip. It reads fast on a phone, it prints on regular paper, and it forces each page to carry one idea. The assignment's structure also fit well, from a hook on the cover to a call to act on page seven.

My audience is people like me: college students who use chatbots every week and have never been asked who made them safe. I want readers to feel two things. First, some discomfort, because the clean answer on the screen has a person behind it. Second, some leverage, because asking where AI comes from is something anyone can do.

I used bold color and big type so the numbers hit first. The school look helps give the reader the feeling that they are learning. Body text stays large with high contrast so more people can read it. I put both sides of the counseling dispute on the page because I wanted the zine to be critical without claiming more than the reporting shows.

I borrowed one idea from football, since that's my world: nobody posts the 200th rep. That's how I think about these workers. The chatbot is the highlight, and they did the reps.

After reading, I want people to credit the labor, ask better questions, and check the sources on the back page.

Attribution & AI Use

  • AI Tool: Claude (Anthropic) for web research, the draft of the research notes
  • Human Contribution: Choosing data labeling and the zine format, the football "nobody posts the 200th rep" angle, direction on tone, and review of the final zine and statements.
  • AI Role: Research assistance, drafting, and layout, not final authorship
  • Tools: Claude; Playwright with Chromium (PDF export).
